In this paper, we present a multi-objective low-carbon multimodal transportation planning problem with fuzzy demand and fuzzy time (MOLCMTPP-FDFT) that minimizes both cost and time while incorporating mandatory carbon emission, carbon tax, carbon trading, and carbon offset policies. Chance constrained programming and interval programming are introduced to formulate the fuzzy demand chance constrained programming model and the fuzzy time interval programming model, respectively. Then, the mathematical model of uncertain MOLCMTPP-FDFT is transformed into a deterministic model. Based on the sparrow search algorithm, t distri­ bution and the concept of Pareto optimality for multi-objective optimization, we also propose a solution strategy for the proposed model. In this algorithm, the number of iterations is used as the degree of freedom of - to update the sparrow location, which strikes a balance between the capabilities of global search and local search. Finally, the proposed algorithm and MOLCMTPP-FDFT are applied to a real case, resulting in a minimum cost of 260730.48 and a time duration of 13.044, which outperform the minimum cost of 268874.88 and minimum time of 18.32 obtained using single-mode transportation. The carbon emissions resulting from the lowest-cost solution obtained using single-mode transportation are 3,198.48, which are signifcantly more than the allowed emis­ sions. Therefore, the proposed algorithm and mathematical model of MOLCMTPP-FDFT are valuable tools for optimizing multimodal transportation route. Additionally, the experimental results not only validate the superior effciency and energy-saving benefts of the proposed multimodal transportation routes in comparison to the actual single-modal transportation, but also demonstrate the applicability of different low-carbon policies.
1. Introduction

With the rapid development of logistics, the implementation of transportation structure adjustment strategy has been vigorously pro­ moted in recent years with the aim of facilitating low-carbon trans­ portation, reducing logistics costs and enhancing transportation effciency (Li, Liu, & Yang, 2021). Multimodal transportation is a crucial component of transportation infrastructure optimization and has emerged as a pivotal logistics mode for numerous enterprises engaged in transport operations (Gurupada, Sankar, & Jose´, 2020). Multimodal transportation refers to the process of transporting cargo to its destina­ tion by utilizing two or more modes of transportation in a coordinated manner (Archetti, Peirano, & Speranza, 2022). The optimization of multimodal transportation effciency has become a central focus of inquiry among numerous scholars (Li et al., 2021; Gurupada, Sankar, & Jos´e, 2020; Laurent, Vallerand, Van der Meer, & Sophie, 2020).

The “Belt and Road” Initiative has stimulated growing industry in­ terest in low-carbon multimodal transportation, which plays a critical role as an organizational form within modern logistics and trans­ portation systems (Qi, Harrod, Psaraftis, & Lang, 2022). The trans­ portation sector accounts for up to $14~\%$ of the total global carbon emissions, with road transportation alone contributing to $70\;\%$ of these emissions. Therefore, it is crucial to consider carbon emission factors in multimodal transportation processes (Maja, & Alan, 2009). In signif­ cant documents, the Chinese government has emphasized that it is necessary to actively adjust the transport structure, promote multimodal transportation, improve the circulation system for green, low-carbon and circular development, and optimize this problem in conjunction with various low-carbon policies (Chen, & Wang, 2016). The LowCarbon Multimodal Transportation Planning Problem (LCMTPP) is the designated term for this issue. Additionally, it takes account into carbon emission allowances under various low-carbon policies and capacity limitations between road segments and transit nodes (Archetti, Peirano, & Speranza, 2022). In this paper, multiple modes of transportation, including trucks, trains and ships, are used to transport goods from the point of origin through multiple cities to the fnal destination. To solve the LCMTPP for a given set of origin–destination transport goods, it is necessary to effectively integrate multiple transport modes and tools, optimize transit nodes and routes, and minimize carbon emissions.

The competition among logistics enterprises is gradually intensifying as transportation means continue to improve, and multimodal trans­ portation networks are progressively enhanced. In order to enhance the core competitiveness of enterprises, it is imperative for them to evaluate the transportation route scheme based on multiple objectives, including minimizing transportation cost and time, reducing carbon emissions, and maximizing customer satisfaction (Adil & Kemal, 2016). Addition­ ally, enterprises should also take into account various uncertain factors in the transportation system such as advance planning of transport schemes, seasonal demand fuctuations, and the infuence of human subjectivity on demand (Zhang, Jin, Yuan, & Zhang, 2021). The trans­ portation process may encounter uncontrollable phenomena and prob­ lems, such as traffc congestion, equipment failure, or extreme weather conditions. These factors contribute to the unpredictability of trans­ portation time. The decision-makers can effectively design strategies that are capable of adapting to changes in the external environment, while minimizing the impact of uncertainties and ensuring the competitiveness of enterprises. This can be achieved by thoroughly considering various uncertainties in the external environment and uti­ lizing multiple evaluation indicators as references. The promotion of low-carbon transportation is effectively achieved through the assess­ ment and formulation of transportation schemes from multiple per­ spectives, even under uncertain conditions (Goncalves, Hsu, & Xu, 2009). Therefore, this paper presents a multi-objective low-carbon multimodal transportation planning problem with fuzzy demand and fuzzy time (MOLCMTPP-FDFT), aiming to minimize both transportation cost and time, while integrating various low-carbon policies into the model.

In order to fnd a feasible solution for balancing transportation cost, carbon emissions, and transportation time under different low-carbon policies. In this paper, a new Pareto-based multi-objective approach is developed, which combines the sparrow search algorithm (SSA) (Xue, & Shen, 2020) and t distribution (Kitagawa, 1953) mutation. The proposed method aims to solve the MOLCMTPP-FDFT and transformation models considering four low-carbon policies, including mandatory carbon emission, carbon tax, carbon trading, and carbon offset. There are some motivations for using the sparrow search algorithm with adaptive t distribution (ATDSSA) to solve this problem which are as follows. Firstly, SSA algorithm is a swarm-based metaheuristic method, which offers several advantages such as minimal parameters, rapid conver­ gence speed, and straightforward implementation. It was primarily utilized for solving deep learning (Fan et al., 2022), machine learning (Jia et al., 2022), feature recognition (Wu, Zhang, Han, Nan, & Li, 2022) and combinatorial optimization problems (Li, & Wang, 2022). It ach­ ieved superior solutions in reasonable computing time (Zhang, Zhang, Ma, & Liu, 2019). Secondly, the swarm optimization algorithm main­ tains a solution pool during a search process (Zhang, Zhang, Ma, & Liu, 2019; Zhang, Liu, Ma, & Zhang, 2020). Thus, swarm optimization al­ gorithms are particularly suitable for fnding trade-off solutions in a single run (Zhang, Zhang, Ma, & Liu, 2019; Zhang, Liu, Ma, & Zhang, 2020). Thirdly, metaheuristics are a general algorithmic framework for fnding solutions to optimization problems, in which local heuristics are guided and adapted to effciently explore the solution space (Zhang, Zhang, Ma, & Liu, 2019; Zhang, Liu, Ma, & Zhang, 2020).

The main contributions of this paper are as follows. Firstly, we have introduced and modeled the MOLCMTPP-FDFT, and transformed model under different low-carbon policies. This enables us to evaluate the impact of different low-carbon policies on the multimodal trans­ portation routing scheme. Secondly, in order to obtain high-quality so­ lutions, ATDSSA was designed to solve the MOLCMTPP-FDFT. This approach not only preserves the characteristics of SSA but also utilizes the number of iterations as freedom of t distribution for balancing global and local search abilities, thereby preventing premature convergence or falling into local optima. Thirdly, chance constrained programming and interval programming are introduced to address uncertain demand and time. The multi-objective fuzzy chance constrained programming model and interval programming model are constructed based on the actual situation. Furthermore, the proposed ATDSSA incorporates the fast nondominated sorting method along with its underlying concept. Finally, we conduct a comprehensive analysis of the performance of our pro­ posed algorithm. As later reported, our method effciently generates trade-off solutions for MOLCMTPP-FDFT under different low-carbon policies.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 provides a brief overview of the existing literatures. Section 3 formally describes MOLCMTPP-FDFT and the transformation model under different lowcarbon policies. Section 4 introduces several fuzzy approaches, including chance constrained programming based on credibility theory, fuzzy variables, and interval programming. Section 5 presents the sparrow search algorithm with adaptive t distributed based on nondominated sorting method. Section 6 describes computational experi­ ments that analyzed the performance and parameter setting of ATDSSA, while also applying the proposed MOLCMTPP-FDFT and transformation models under different low-carbon policies in a real case study. Section 7 summarizes the impact of different low-carbon policies on multimodal transportation routing decisions.
2. Literature review

The aim of this section is to provide a short but comprehensive overview of work related to low-carbon multimodal transportation planning problems, multi-objective optimization techniques, and fuzzy approaches.

In recent years, the topic of low-carbon in multimodal transportation has attracted signifcant attention from researchers. Li and Sun (2022) addressed the problem with demand uncertainty and carbon trading price randomness by formulating a robust stochastic optimization model for container multimodal transportation with minimum total cost as the objective function. They also developed a hybrid freworks algorithm with gravitational search operator (FAGSO) to solve it, which demon­ strated its effectiveness. (Li, & Sun, 2022). Cheng (2022) established a multimodal transportation planning problem model with the objective of minimizing the total transportation cost, which includes costs of transportation, transit, waiting and carbon emission, respectively (Cheng, 2022). To solve this model effectively, a genetic algorithm incorporating reservation and immigration strategies was employed. This approach provides decision support for selecting an optimal multimodal transportation scheme (Cheng, 2022). Liao, Tseng and Lu (2009) compared the carbon emissions of only truck transportation with the carbon emissions of multimodal transportation. The fndings revealed that employing multimodal transportation for freight trans­ portation can signifcantly reduce carbon dioxide emissions (Liao, Tseng, & Lu, 2009). Behnam, Joseph, Alok and Ali (2015) proposed a strategic supply chain planning model that integrates economic and carbon emission targets within the framework of a carbon tax policy. This nonlinear supply chain planning model is solved using an improved cross-entropy method (Behnam, Joseph, Alok, & Ali, 2015).

There are few studies on low-carbon multimodal transportation planning problems involving multiple objectives in the existing litera­ ture. The main reason is that multi-objective problems are more diffcult than single-objective ones. Most multimodal transportation planning problems with multiple objectives are solved by linear weighting into single objective problems. Kalinina, Olsson and Larsson (2013) estab­ lished an optimization model, which aims to minimize transportation time, cost, and carbon emissions in multimodal transportation planning problem (Kalinina, Olsson & Larsson, 2013). Siu, Lam and Gu (2015) developed innovative methods for designing enhanced intermodal transportation networks provided by freight integrators. They con­ structed a bi-objective optimization model to minimize both cost and transportation time, and utilized CPLEX, which is a commonly used solver for mixed integer linear programming (MILP) problems, to fnd Pareto solutions (Siu, Lam, & Gu, 2015). With the increase in transit nodes, the combined routes of different transportation modes grow exponentially, resulting in more complex calculations (Xiong & Wang, 2014). Exact algorithms and optimization solvers can only handle smallscale combinatorial optimization problems, making it challenging to provide solutions for large-scale problems within a limited computing time (Zhang, Liu, Ma, & Zhang, 2020). Therefore, intelligent optimiza­ tion algorithms that can provide approximate optimal solutions to largescale problems within an ideal time, have widely used by many scholars (Zhang, Liu, Ma, & Zhang, 2020). For instance, genetic algorithm (Xie, & Cao, 2021; Fattahi, & Behnamian, 2021), simulated annealing algorithm (Oudani, 2021), and freworks algorithm (Mouna, & Sadok, 2017) have demonstrated satisfactory results in solving multi-objective multimodal transportation planning problems.

Besides, scholars have focused on these multimodal transportation planning problems under uncertainty. Considering the uncertain factors into multimodal transportation process can reduce the environmental impacts on the transportation schemes. The multimodal transportation planning problem under uncertainty mainly includes uncertainties in transportation time, volume, and customer demand. Uncertain variables can be classifed into random variables and fuzzy variables (Shi, Bou­ douh, & Grunder, 2017) with different expressions used in routing optimization problems. Stochastic programming is commonly employed to solve problems involving random variables, such as robust optimi­ zation (Iyengar, 2005) and auxiliary variable method (Bertsimas, & Sim, 2004). Triangular fuzzy numbers, trapezoidal fuzzy numbers and in­ terval numbers are typically utilized to represent fuzzy variables. Furthermore, expected value models (Xu, Yan, & Li, 2011), chance constrained programming (Messaoud, 2021), and interval programming (Subulan, 2020; Robers, & Ben-Israel, 1969) are applied to transform fuzzy variables into certain ones.

Kalinina, Olsson and Larsson (2013) used a fuzzy chance constraint model to solve the multimodal transportation with uncertain time. Fazayeli, Eydi and Kamalabadi (2018) proposed a mixed integer math­ ematical fuzzy model for the multimodal transportation planning problem with fuzzy demand. A fuzzy $\upalpha$ -cut technology is used to trans­ form the fuzzy demand an expectation interval, and transformed the original fuzzy model into an auxiliary deterministic one. Zhang (2022) considered the optimization of multimodal transportation routing under the double uncertainty in both time window and demand by using trapezoidal fuzzy variables to represent these uncertainties. The fuzzy chance constrained programming was applied to solve the bi-objective fuzzy model. (Zhang, 2022).

The research on MOLCMTPP-FDFT under different low-carbon pol­ icies is limited, highlighting the need for extensive investigation in this area. This includes employing hybrid methods that utilize various heu­ ristic evolutionary/swarm algorithms, exact methods, and local search techniques to enhance solution quality and/or reduce computational time (Zhang, Zhang, Ma, & Liu, 2019; Zhang, Liu, Ma, & Zhang, 2020). In this paper, we aim to construct MOLCMTPP-FDFT under various lowcarbon policies such as mandatory carbon emission, carbon tax, carbon trading and carbon offset. To address these problems, we propose Pareto-based sparrow search algorithm with adaptive t distributed. Through case analysis, we discussed the infuence of different lowcarbon policies on multimodal transportation routing decisions. These fndings provide valuable insights for decision-makers involved in implementing low-carbon multimodal transportation practices and assist governmental bodies and relevant organizations in formulating future low-carbon policies.

Finally, Table 1 classifes and summarizes literature mentioned above from the aspects of problem categories, uncertainty components of problems, transportation mode, optimization objectives, carbon emissions, low-carbon policies and solution methodology (Subulan, 2020). As shown in Table 1, the literature on multimodal transportation planning problem is abundant. However, there remains a scarcity of studies that consider multiple objectives, various uncertainties, and multiple low-carbon policies. Most of existing literature have concen­ trated on transportation in deterministic environments or have only taken one uncertain factor into account. They have also neglected lowcarbon policies when estimating carbon emissions, which makes them inaccurate representations of reality. When solving the low-carbon multimodal transportation planning problem, various uncertain fac­ tors and multiple low-carbon policies need to be considered simulta­ neously in order to accurately refect reality.
3. Mathematical model for MOLCMTPP-FDFT

The MOLCMTPP-FDFT refers particularly to the problem of effec­ tively transporting a batch of cargo from the origin to the destination via a variety of transportation means, such as trucks, ships, trains, and planes, while taking fuzzy time and demand into account. In this com­ plex transportation system, the effective and rational integration of various transfer nodes and transportation modes is crucial in minimizing the transportation time, cost, and carbon emissions that are converted to costs and associated with low-carbon policies, such as mandatory carbon emission, carbon tax, carbon trading and carbon compensation.
3.1. The basic MOLCMTPP-FDFT– model I

Logistics enterprise needs to adopt multiple transportation means to transport some goods with uncertain demand from the origin to the destination through various transit nodes with the minimum trans­ portation cost and time. In response to national initiatives promoting low-carbon transportation, these enterprises must develop correspond­ ing schemes for low-carbon transportation under different low-carbon policies. To facilitate model construction, we make the following as­ sumptions: (1) goods cannot be disassembled in transportation process; (2) selecting at most one transportation mode between two transit nodes; (3) each transit node can only carry out mode conversion at most once; (4) capacity constraint should be considered for each trans­ portation section and transit node; (5) external factors such as weather conditions, equipment failure or cargo damage are not taken into account.

The MOLCMTPP-FDFT considered in this paper is a combinatorial problem. 3.2. The MOLCMTPP-FDFT under different carbon policies

The low-carbon multimodal transportation model with fuzzy de­ mand and fuzzy time is transformed under mandatory carbon emissions, carbon tax, carbon trading and carbon offset. These are respectively referred to as Model II, Model III, Model IV and Model V. The following subsections provide a detailed description.
3.2.1. The model under mandatory carbon emission policy – model II

The government’s mandated regulations on carbon emission require that logistics transportation should be conducted strictly in compliance with the carbon emission allowance. Therefore, Model II retains the objectives and constraints in Model I, while ensuring that the maximum carbon emissions cannot be exceeded under this policy.
Constraint (14) means that the total carbon emission must be less than the upper bound of emission stipulated by the government.
3.2.2. The model under carbon tax policy – model III

Carbon tax is defned as the cost associated with carbon emissions, which includes a fxed tax rate $\gamma$ multiplied by total carbon emissions and added to the total cost $Z_{1}$ . Therefore, in Model III, the objective function should incorporate the cost of carbon emissions into the total cost using equation (15), while still satisfying constraints (4) \~ (13).

4. The fuzzy approach

Currently, stochastic programming, fuzzy programming and interval programming are commonly used to deal with uncertain parameters in routing optimization. Interval programming belongs to the category of fuzzy programming. In generally, less data can be used to evaluate the probability distribution of demand for the decision makers, resulting in a less feasible stochastic programming. Existing literature commonly employs triangular fuzzy variables, trapezoidal fuzzy variables, and in­ terval numbers as methods to represent those uncertain variables. The maximum membership degree of triangular fuzzy numbers can only correspond to one value, which is only applicable to a clearly defned range. In contrast, trapezoidal fuzzy numbers are more fexible, and the maximum membership degree of trapezoidal fuzzy numbers can corre­ spond to an interval, which allows different decision makers to hold varying opinions on the most likely value. Some scholars have proposed that the trapezoidal fuzzy numbers can better represent the fuzzy de­ mand in actual situation. In addition, weather, road conditions and personnel habits all impact transportation time. It is possible to roughly determine the time range for each road section and transit node based on past experience and recent road conditions. Therefore, the fexible trapezoidal fuzzy number is used to represent fuzzy demand while using interval numbers for dealing fuzzy time.
4.1. General fuzzy measure
The General Fuzzy (GF) measure, proposed by Xu and Zhou (2011), utilized to quantify the probability of fuzzy phenomena. Let $(\Theta,P(\Theta)$ ,

$P o s$ ) denote the possibility space, where $\mathcal{B}$ represents an event in $P(\Theta)$ , and $P o s\{\mathcal{B}\}$ indicates the possibility of event $\mathcal{B}$ occurring. Moreover, the necessity of event $\mathcal{B}$ occurring can be determined as $N e c\{B\}\,=$ $1-P o s\{\mathcal{B}^{C}\}$ , where ${\mathcal{B}}^{C}$ represents the complement of event $\mathcal{B}$ . The general fuzzy measure can be expressed as a convex combination of possibility $(P o s)$ and necessity (Nec), yielding $G F\{{\mathcal{B}}\}\,=\,N e c\{{\mathcal{B}}\}\,+$ $\mathcal{L}(P o s\{\mathcal{B}\}-N e c\{\mathcal{B}\})=\mathcal{L}P o s\{\mathcal{B}\}-(1-\mathcal{L})N e c\{\mathcal{B}\}$ . The parameter $\mathcal{L}(0\leq\mathcal{L}\leq1)$ ) serves as a determinant of the decision maker’s incli­ nation towards optimism or pessimism (Nasim, Mohsen, Hosseinzadeh, & Hasan, 2022; Xu & Zhou, 2011, 2013).

Moreover, triangular and trapezoidal fuzzy variables for handling uncertain demand is more suitable since they are better aligned with the actual problem description (Dong, & Wan, 2018). Additionally, Zhang (2022) provides several reasons why trapezoidal fuzzy variables outperform triangular ones. Firstly, the trapezoidal fuzzy variables are allowed to have multiple most probable values, which meet the actual situation that different decision makers and experts have different opinions on the most probable values. Secondly, the uncertain param­ eters are expressed as trapezoidal fuzzy variables to make the decision more fexible. Finally, by signifcantly reducing the upper and lower bounds of the fuzzy variable, trapezoidal fuzzy variables can be conve­ niently approximated as triangular fuzzy variables (Zhang, 2022). 5.3. Sparrow search algorithm with adaptive t distribution (ATDSSA)

ATDSSA incorporates adaptive t distribution into SSA, and its inno­ vation point is that the number of iterations is used as the degree of freedom parameter of $t$ distribution to perturb the sparrow location. In the initial iterations, the mutation of the t distribution is equivalent to that of the Cauchy distribution, which has better global search ability. As the iterations progress, the degrees of freedom of t distribution variation increase, which is similar with Gaussian distribution and has good local exploration ability. The number of iterations was utilized to adjust the degrees of freedom in the t distribution, achieving a balance between local and global search and enhancing the optimization per­ formance of the algorithm. Moreover, the non-dominated sorting and mutation operations in NSGA-II are also employed to solve the proposed mathematical model of MOLCMTPP-FDFT and improve the optimization performance of ATDSSA. The individual locations are updated adap­ tively by t distribution using Eq. (38).

The t distribution is utilized to enhance the SSA. Firstly, the algo­ rithm parameters are confgured, and the initial population is randomly generated. The individual objective function value of the population is calculated, and the Pareto solution set is selected. The population in­ dividuals are categorized as producers and scroungers based on the pareto front. Additionally, the updates for the locations of producers and scroungers are performed separately. The t distribution mutation oper­ ation is performed on the population when the density value of the t distribution exceeds a random number. The loop terminates when the maximum number of iterations is reached, and the optimal solution set is output. text: 5.3.2. Fast construction method of Pareto non-dominated solution

Non-dominated sorting method is a common solution strategy for multi-objective optimization problems, and it has been described in detail in many literatures. This paper adopted the fast non-dominated sorting algorithm (FNSA) proposed by Deb in 2002 to solve the multiobjective problem (Deb, Agrawal, Pratap, & Meyarivan, 2002). Deb, Agrawal, Pratap and Meyarivan (2002) provided a comprehensive defnition and detailed explanation of FNSA. The FNSA is extensively employed in the renowned Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II). FNSA partitions the merged population into multiple layers of non-dominated fronts, which furnish crucial individual-level infor­ mation for generating population of the succeeding generation and accomplishing the selection operation. The time complexity of FNSA is $O(N M^{2})$ , where $N$ represents the number of objective functions, and $M$ denotes the population size. Algorithm 1 presents the pseudocode for FNSA. Firstly, the non-dominated solution set $\acute{I}$ and dominated solution set $I^{'}$ are initially defned as empty sets (line 2). Lines 3–18 depict the process of non-dominated sorting for all individuals within the popu­ lation. The individual $I_{i}$ added to the dominant solution set $I^{'}$ if there exists an individual $I_{j}$ that dominates $I_{i}$ $\left(I_{j}\prec I_{i}\&I_{j}\neq I_{i}\right)$ (lines 4–14). Otherwise, individual $I_{i}$ is added to the non-dominated solution set $\dot{I}$ (line 16), and this process is repeated until all individuals are assigned to either the non-dominated or dominated solution set. The non-dominated solution set and the dominated solution set are merged into a new set $\vec{I}^{*}$ by prioritizing the non-dominated solutions. Then, those sets $\boldsymbol{I}^{*},\boldsymbol{I}$ and $I^{^{\prime}}$ are subsequently generated as output (lines 19–20).

5.3.4. t Distribution mutation

The degree of freedom of the t distribution is determined by the number of iterations, and its density function value $P(t)$ is compared with a random number rand. If $P(t)>$ rand, a node different from the destination is randomly selected from the updated route and $t$ distri­ bution variation is performed, Otherwise, a feasible solution is gener­ ated randomly. The steps for t distribution mutation are as follows:
Step 1: calculate the local objectives of different transportation modes from the mutation node to all forward nodes, respectively.
Step 2: the two objective values are weighted linearly to form the total ftness cost, fitness $=Z_{1}+Z_{2}\times\,c_{\mathrm{time}}$ , where $c_{\mathrm{time}}$ means unit time cost.
Step 3: select the forward node and transportation mode that have the minimum local ftness as the forward local route of the mutation node.
Step 4: take the selected forward node as the new mutation node, and repeat Steps $1\sim3$ until the mutation node is the destination to end the cycle.

text: 6.3. Effectiveness of the proposed t distribution mutation in ATDSSA

The effectiveness of the t distribution mutation update strategy in ATDSSA is verifed in this subsection. To determine whether incorpo­ rating a t distribution mutation operation in solving the MOLCMTPPFDFT problem enhances the performance of ATDSSA, the optimization algorithm SSA1 is employed, which is used to solve the aforementioned instance while keeping other parameters and factors unchanged.

SSA1: the number of iterations serves as the degree of freedom for the t distribution, which is utilized to update the population’s location during the counterattack phase when an individual is at risk.

See Fig. 8. shows the non-dominated solutions obtained using ATDSSA and SSA1 after 10 runs, respectively. When the non-dominated frontier is closer to the lower left corner, it indicates a higher quality of solutions. As shown in Fig. 8, it is evident that non-dominated solutions obtained by ATDSSA are closer to the lower left corner than those ob­ tained using SSA1, which indicates that utilizing the number of itera­ tions as a degree of freedom to update population locations during danger encounters is an effective strategy that enhances effectiveness of ATDSSA.
6.4. Comparison and analysis with other intelligent algorithms

In order to verify the performance of the proposed ATDSSA, we conducted a comparative analysis with other state-of-the-art algorithms such as grey wolf optimization (GWO) (Mirjalili, Mirjalili, & Lewis, 2014), gravity search algorithm, (GSA) (Rashedi, Nezamabadi-pour, & Saryazdi, 2009), particle swarm optimization (PSO) (Zhang, Liu, Ma, & Zhang, 2020) and NSGA-II (Deb, Agrawal, Pratap, & Meyarivan, 2002). The results obtained using each algorithm under carbon tax policy are shown in Table 12, which includes representative non-dominated solu­ tions $I_{g b e s t1}$ with the minimum cost and $I_{g b e s t2}$ with minimum trans­ portation time, average cost $Z_{1-A V G}$ , average transportation time $Z_{2-A V G}$ , average carbon emission $Q_{A V G}$ of the non-dominant solutions, and CPU time in seconds.

From Table 12, it is easy to know that the non-dominated solutions obtained by GWO, GSA, PSO and SSA are inferior to those obtained by ATDSSA. Although both ATDSSA and NSGA-II can obtain better solu­ tions, ATDSSA needs less computation time while ensuring the same high-quality solutions. The results presented in Table 12 not only indi­ cate that the ATDSSA is a very competitive algorithm for solving the multimodal transportation planning problem, but also demonstrate that the t distribution mutation operation effectively improves the perfor­ mance of SSA.
6.5. Experimental results under different low-carbon policies

The proposed ATDSSA is also used to solve the MOLCMTPP-FDFT under different low-carbon policies including mandatory carbon emis­ sion, carbon tax, carbon trading, and carbon offset. The non-dominated solutions and their corresponding average values obtained under each low-carbon policy are presented in Table 13. Comparing the solutions shown in Table 13, it is easy to observe that the solutions obtained under carbon tax policy have the lowest carbon emission, but their trans­ portation costs are also signifcantly higher, which indicates that while the implementation of a carbon tax policy can effectively reduce carbon emissions, it may also lead to a largely increase in transportation costs. Carbon offset has the weakest impact on the reduction of carbon emis­ sion, and the solutions obtained under it have higher transportation costs. The emission reduction effect of mandatory carbon emission and carbon trading lies between that of carbon tax and carbon offset. Although the transportation costs and carbon emissions of solutions obtained using mandatory carbon emission are slightly lower than those obtained using carbon trading, their transportation time is compara­ tively longer.

text: 7. Conclusion

The mathematical models are developed for multimodal trans­ portation planning problem with fuzzy demand and fuzzy time under different carbon emission policies, aiming to minimize both cost and time of low-carbon transportation. It is possible to provide more economical and environmentally friendly transportation selections for the multimodal transportation routing problem under different lowcarbon policies by incorporating unpredictable factors and the impact of transport and transit capacities. Furthermore, the original SSA has been improved to solve the MOLCMTPP-FDFT by utilizing the number of it­ erations as a degree of freedom for t distribution, which effectively balances local and global search capabilities of the SSA and compensates for its susceptibility to local optima. The experimental results demon­ strate that mandatory carbon emission and carbon tax policies can successfully reduce carbon emissions, which provides appropriate ap­ proaches for urgent reduction in carbon emissions. The implementation of carbon trading policy can partially alleviate enterprise costs, thereby facilitating the early-stage promotion of low-carbon transportation practices.

ATDSSA has also been compared with other state-of-the-art intelli­ gent optimization algorithms, such as GWO, PSO and NSGA-II. Although ATDSSA and NSGA-II obtain the same non-dominated solutions, the computation time required by ATDSSA is shorter than that of GSA, PSO and NSGA-II. Therefore, we can conclude that the proposed ATDSSA is a very competitive algorithm for solving multi-objective optimization problems. It can also be used to solve other multi-objective combina­ torial optimization problems, such as multi-objective location routing problem, multi-objective vehicle routing problem, and multi-objective facility location problem. Additionally, the proposed mathematical model of MOLCMTPP-FDFT can obtain reasonable transportation routes while ensuring the minimization of cost, carbon emission and trans­ portation time, which is helpful to the promotion of low-carbon trans­ portation network.

The ATDSSA is a competitive algorithm that can effectively solve not only the multi-objective multimodal transportation planning problems, but also vehicle routing problem, location-routing problem and other combinatorial optimization problems. The mathematical model of MOLCMTPP-FDFT can provide cost-effective, environmentally-friendly and effcient transportation solution for logistics. However, this study also has two primary limitations. Firstly, due to the limited scope of this paper, a theoretical analysis of the convergence of ATDSS was not conducted. Secondly, there are many uncertainties in realistic trans­ portation networks, but this study only considers fuzzy demand and time.

To extend this work and overcome its limitations, the following works can be done in the future:(1) exploring some effective methods to balance the global search and local search to further improve the per­ formance of the algorithm. (2) proposing other methods to deal with uncertain variables, and reducing the impact of environmental changes on routing decision. (3) considering the low-carbon multimodal trans­ portation of special products such as dangerous products, emergency supplies, and perishable food.
